column2: On the authority of Abū Saʿīd Saʿd ibn Mālik ibn Sinān al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “There is to be no harm and no reciprocating harm.” A ḥasan hadith,

reported by Ibn Mājah, al-Dāraquṭnī and others with a connected chain, and reported by Mālik in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ as mursal, from ʿAmr ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, omitting Abū Saʿīd. It has routes that strengthen one another.

This hadith contains one of the principles of the Sharīʿah: the removal of harm (ḍarar) and reciprocal harm (ḍirār). It is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition of harm and reciprocal harm. Harm may come from a person intentionally or unintentionally,

while reciprocal harm is with intention. The ḥāfiẓ Ibn Rajab said in Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam (2/212): “They differed as to whether there is a difference between the two words—I mean ḍarar and ḍirār—or not.

Some said they mean the same thing, by way of emphasis. The well-known view is that there is a difference between them. Then it was said that ḍarar is the noun and ḍirār the act, so the meaning is that harm itself is negated in the Sharīʿah, and so is inflicting harm without right. It was also said
that ḍarar is inflicting harm on another by something from which one benefits oneself, and ḍirār is inflicting harm on another by something from which one has no benefit,
like someone who withholds what does him no harm [to give] while the one denied is harmed by it; a group, among them Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, preferred this view.

It was also said that ḍarar is harming someone who has not harmed you, and ḍirār is harming someone who has harmed you in an impermissible way. In any case, the Prophet ﷺ negated only harm and reciprocal harm without right.

As for inflicting harm on someone rightfully—either because he has transgressed the limits of Allah and is punished in proportion to his crime, or because he has wronged himself and others and the wronged party seeks to answer him with justice—this is certainly not what is meant. What is meant is inflicting harm without right, and this is of two kinds.
The first is where there is no aim other than harming that other person; there is no doubt that this is ugly and unlawful.

The prohibition of causing harm has come in the Qurʾān in several places, among them regarding bequests; Allah the Exalted said: ‘…after any bequest he has made or debt, without causing harm’ [al-Nisāʾ 4:12].”

He went on to say (2/217): “The second kind is where he has another valid aim, such as disposing of his property in a way that benefits him, and this extends to harming someone else; or preventing someone else from benefiting from his property in order to keep it for himself, and the one prevented is harmed by that.”
An explanation of the perfection and excellence of the Sharīʿah in removing harm and the infliction of harm.
A Muslim should neither harm others nor return harm to them.
